section_1.content: Briefly revisit the 'Bell Curve' (Normal Distribution). Emphasize that it is symmetric, defined by mean and variance, and appears naturally in many physical phenomena.
section_1.example: Visual: An animation showing height distribution of a large group of students forming a smooth bell curve shape.

section_2.title: The Problem: Randomness and Chaos
section_2.content: Introduce the concept that in the real world, data is often 'messy' or non-normal (e.g., uniform or skewed distributions). How do we predict the behavior of sums or averages from these chaotic sources?
section_2.example: Visual: A virtual 'dice-rolling machine' producing a flat, uniform distribution where every outcome (1-6) has an equal chance.

section_3.title: The Mechanism: The Convergence Principle
section_3.content: State the Central Limit Theorem: As the sample size (n) increases, the distribution of the sample mean will approach a Normal Distribution, regardless of the shape of the original population distribution.
section_3.example: Visual: Animation showing the sampling distribution of 1, 2, 5, and 30 dice rolls. Watch the histogram morph from 'flat' to 'jagged' to a 'perfect Bell Curve'.

section_4.title: Real-World Application: The 'Robo-Delivery' Fleet
section_4.content: Demonstrate the power of CLT using a delivery robot example. Even if individual robots have erratic delivery times, the 'average' delivery time of a fleet follows a predictable pattern.
section_4.example: Visual: 100 robots have highly unpredictable battery depletion rates (skewed distribution). By taking the average of 50 samples, we can accurately predict the 'fleet average' to ensure city-wide logistics planning.

section_5.title: Summary & Critical Takeaway
section_5.content: Reinforce that the CLT is the bridge between raw, noisy data and statistical inference. Key condition: n must be sufficiently large (usually n > 30).
section_5.example: Visual: A side-by-side summary graphic showing the 'Chaos' of raw data on the left transforming into the 'Order' of the Normal Distribution on the right.

    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"

        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text("- " + line, font_size=20, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                # Shift right-side grid to the right (x=2 to x=7)
                x = 2.5 + j * 0.8
                y = 2.0 - i * 0.8
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
